newsitem.title: BELGIUM: FOCUS - Mixed fortunes for European truck makers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Mixed fortunes for European truck makers.

text.p: Leading European truck makers Mercedes and Scania on Friday reported strong 1996 sales but another major manufacturer, Volvo, had a miserable year due to plunging U.S. sales.

At the Brussels truck show, Mercedes-Benz AG truck unit chief Kurt Lauk said sales climbed to 348,200 units last year from 320,100, helped by the company's light trucks and vans, and were likely to rise above 350,000 in 1997.
Scania said its share of the market in Western Europe rose to 15.5 percent between January and November 1996 from 14.5 percent a year earlier.
But at fellow Swedish truck maker Volvo, 1996 sales dived 17 percent to 63,682 due to a fall in North and Latin America.

In Europe Volvo's truck unit consolidated its position as the second largest manufacturer of heavy trucks. Volvo increased its market share for heavy trucks to 16.8 percent in November 1996 from 16.2 percent in 1995.
Deliveries in Europe of 35,030 trucks last year were little changed from 35,190 in 1995.
In North America Volvo sold 16,855 trucks last year, down 38 percent from 27,092 in 1995. In Latin America sales fell 36 percent to 4,982 trucks from 7,798 the previous year.

At Mercedes' truck unit revenue slipped to 31.5 million marks ($19.7 million) from 31.6 million despite the higher sales. But Lauk said the unit was positioned for higher profits and that by the end of the decade it would be able to make a profit in all its operations.
He said Mercedes had been hit especially hard by weak European demand for heavy trucks and had seen its market share slip in that sector in recent years, analysts said.

Urban Erdtman, head of Scania's European sales, said market share was growing in the largest market block -- Britain, Germany and France -- which together account for about 60 percent of all heavy trucks registered in Europe.
On these markets, the first 11 months showed a two percent reduction in total registrations compared with the previous year while Scania increased its figures by just over four percent.
"Scania secured almost 12 percent of the total market within this block. The ambition is to take additional market shares," Erdtman said.
Scania was concentrating its efforts in Germany and France on consolidating its position through investments in and reorganising the dealership network.
The company said statistics for 1996 showed Scania increased its market share in Britain to 18.6 percent from 16.6, while market share in Sweden rose to 48.3 percent from 43.6 a year ago.
